source.title: Analysis of Interpolating Regression Models and the Double Descent Phenomenon

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Minor extraction and symbol-formatting issues are visible, but they do not prevent reading the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: Tests double-descent behavior with simulated interpolating least-squares regression models rather than deep networks, and compares test NMSE across model orders and model structures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports NMSE results for its own simulations and inverse-smallest-singular-value plots. Cited findings from other papers are not recorded as rows. The ridge-regression discussion is analytical; it does not report a numerical ridge experiment.
record.test_reason: The study simulates minimum-norm least-squares regression with complex-exponential bases. It sweeps model order across the interpolation threshold (N=10) and reports test NMSE with and without label noise. These results bear on V4, whether risk falls again past interpolation outside deep networks, and on the noise-driven part of V6. It adds an analytical account of why the peak sits at n=N.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors tie double descent to the inverse smallest singular value of the regression matrix. A near-singular matrix at n=N produces double descent in test NMSE at points away from the training inputs. Pseudo-inverse overparametrized solutions are reasonable only if the true parameter is near the regression matrix's row space. Robust overparametrized models need a model class that keeps the smallest singular value large.
record.recipe_differences: Uses simulated minimum-norm least-squares regression with complex-exponential basis functions, model-order sweeps, and NMSE, rather than deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies with basis-function ordering, data-generating function, noisy versus noise-free training data, and test offset epsilon (0 or 0.5).

fits_no_version.finding: The inverse smallest singular value of the regression matrix peaks at n=N. Its curve qualitatively matches the test NMSE under linear ordering and is much smaller under optimal ordering. A theorem shows sigma_min is non-increasing for n<N and non-decreasing for n>=N.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Along the model-order axis in linear regression, the double-descent peak location and size track the conditioning (smallest singular value) of the regression matrix, which depends on basis ordering.

record.problems: The numerical examples use N=10 and simulated data. Curves are presented as plots without reported uncertainty estimates. The text states 500 training datasets were generated per case, but gives no error bars or confidence intervals. Some cases evaluate at the training input points (epsilon=0), so they do not assess generalization away from those points.

untested.parts: No deep networks. Only linearly parametrized regression.
Sample count is fixed at N=10.
No effective-complexity measure across size, epochs and samples. Only a singular-value diagnostic on the model-order axis.

Single noise variance (0.1); no noise-level sweep. No multiple or triple peaks. Ridge regularization is analysed only analytically (variance falls with lambda, shrinkage adds bias); there is no numerical tuned-ridge test.
No re-expression against an effective number of parameters.
Only one model family (complex-exponential bases, two orderings). N=10.

record.verdict_notes: Results are figure-only. Means are taken over 500 Monte Carlo datasets per case, with no uncertainty reported. Cases B and D evaluate at the training inputs and are not test risk. The text's 'Corollary 2' is presumably Corollary 1. The joint C/D sentence about the peak at n=N most plausibly refers to Figure 3. The V5 label in the record was dropped because the singular-value diagnostic is not an effective-complexity measure. This resolves the reader's validation issue.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses linearly parametrized regression models, not deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
The number of training samples is fixed at N=10; the study does not test increasing the sample count near the interpolation threshold.
Tests simulated linearly parametrized regression models and two orderings of complex-exponential basis functions, not a broad range of model classes.
Examines the smallest singular value in relation to model order, but does not test a single effective-complexity measure across size, epochs, and sample count.
Compares noisy and noise-free data in simulations, but does not sweep noise levels, test multiple or triple peaks, or numerically test optimally tuned regularization.
Does not re-express results using an effective number of parameters or show that the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

statements.correction: Linear ordering: interpolation peak at n=N=10 in Cases A and C. Optimal ordering, Case C: best noisy NMSE at n=10; slight deterioration at higher orders. Optimal ordering, Case A: noisy performance comparable to noise-free performance; substantially smaller variance.
statements.problem: Peak removal is supported explicitly for Case C. For Case A, the text establishes reduced variance and improved NMSE but does not describe the optimal-ordering curve sufficiently to verify peak removal.

statements.correction: Optimal ordering produces a well-conditioned regression matrix and reduces variance. Case C has best noisy NMSE at n=N=10 and slightly worse performance beyond it. These results support conditioning-dependent variance effects; noise sufficiency is not asserted by V6.
statements.problem: The regression finding does not challenge V6: a noise-driven or variance-driven peak does not imply that adding noise must create a peak. Case A's peak absence also cannot be verified from the extracted curve.

statements.correction: Case A, linear ordering: noisy NMSE exhibits double descent with a peak at n=N=10. Optimal ordering: noisy NMSE is comparable to noise-free NMSE; the inverse smallest singular value and variance are substantially smaller.
statements.problem: The cited Case A comparison establishes strong variance suppression, but complete peak removal is not stated or readable in the supplied text.
